questions.question: What is considered one of the earliest known examples of animation?
options: The Phenakistoscope spinning disc device (1831)
Leonardo da Vinci's sketches of birds in flight (1510)
Muybridge's photographic sequence of a galloping horse (1878)
A pottery bowl from Shahr-e Sukhteh, Iran (~3200 BCE) showing a goat leaping
questions.explanation: At [01:28], the lecturer explains that people have always been interested in depicting motion. The Shahr-e Sukhteh pottery bowl (~3200 BCE) is one of the oldest known animations — a sequence of images painted around the bowl showing a goat leaping toward a tree. When the bowl spins, the images animate.

questions.question: What scientific question motivated Muybridge's 1878 photographic film "Sallie Gardner"?
options: Animal motion observer effect
Horse legs all off ground?
Camera vs hand-drawing speed
Eye perception >12 fps?
questions.explanation: At [03:44], the lecturer states: "The first real film was done by Muybridge who was trying to resolve a very simple question: when a horse gallops, do all four legs ever leave the ground at the same time?" He set up a series of cameras triggered by trip wires to capture the motion — and yes, all four legs do leave the ground.

questions.question: What was historically significant about Ivan Sutherland's "Sketchpad" (1963)?
options: First digital computer animation
First physics-based character sim
First feature-length CGI film
First ray tracing in graphics
questions.explanation: At [07:24], the lecturer says: "The first digital computer animation was something called Sketchpad developed by Ivan Sutherland, and this was a really landmark development in not only computer graphics but also human-computer interaction." Like Muybridge's film, it started as a scientific/technical tool rather than entertainment.

questions.question: What was historically notable about Lotte Reiniger's "Die Abenteuer des Prinzen Achmed" (1926)?
options: First CGI in a film
First feature animation
First motion capture film
First spline interpolation use
questions.explanation: At [05:21], the lecturer describes Reiniger's film as "the first feature-length animation" — made using silhouette cut-out puppet technique, predating Disney's Snow White by over a decade. It demonstrates that animation as an art form preceded digital tools by many decades.

questions.question: What is the "beta phenomenon" in the perception of motion?
options: Retinal afterimage ~1/24 sec
Phi phenomenon fills gaps
Brain retains motion memory
Soap opera effect at high fps
questions.intuition: The old "persistence of vision" theory said the eye itself acts like a slow camera with motion blur. That's wrong. The eye resets almost instantly. It's the BRAIN that holds the record of recent motion and uses it to create a sense of continuity — which is why movies work at 24fps even though real motion is continuous.
questions.explanation:
At [13:54], the lecturer states: "More modern psychological explanations are things like the beta phenomenon — you do have this kind of persistence of motion but that record of what was happening is kept not in the eyeball but in the brain." The original "persistence of vision" theory has been debunked.

applied from camera doesn't really apply to our eye .

questions.question: What is the "phi phenomenon" in motion perception?
options: Two images appear to move
Motion-induced brightness gain
Brain anticipates motion onset
Minimum smooth fps ≈ 24
questions.explanation: At [14:25], the lecturer explains: "There's also something called the phi phenomenon, which is that the brain anticipates motion — there are visual cues that you see in nature that make you feel like motion is going to occur." Together, beta and phi explain why animation works: the brain actively constructs the sense of motion rather than passively recording it.

questions.question: What is the traditional hand-drawn animation workflow?
options: Senior draws keys; junior tweens
One artist draws all frames
Each animator draws all frames
Computer draws keys; humans tween
questions.explanation: At [16:03], the lecturer describes: "To generate this motion, a senior artist sits down and draws keyframes — frames that highlight key events. Then an apprentice fills in the rest, drawing inbetweens." This is the origin of the word "tweening" and directly motivates computer animation: the inbetween work is tedious and perfect for automation.

questions.question: What are the three basic techniques in computer animation?
options: Keyframing, motion capture, simulation
Spline interpolation, particle systems, skeletal rigging
Rasterization, ray tracing, path tracing
Forward kinematics, inverse kinematics, physics simulation
questions.explanation: At [17:15], the lecturer outlines: "There are a lot of different basic techniques for computer animation: artist-directed (e.g., keyframing), data-driven (e.g., motion capture), and procedural (e.g., simulation)." These map roughly to how much human artistic input vs. automated computation is involved.

questions.question: What is the core idea of keyframing in computer animation?
options: Hand-drawing and scanning every frame
Full physical simulation of all forces
Capturing actor motion with reflective markers
Specifying key events; computer interpolates
questions.explanation: At [18:30], the lecturer explains: "Basic idea: specify important events only — computer fills in the rest via interpolation/approximation. 'Events' don't have to be position — could be color, light intensity, camera zoom..." This is the digital version of the senior artist drawing keyframes, with the computer doing the apprentice's tweening work.

questions.question: What is the problem with piecewise linear interpolation for animation?
options: It requires too many keyframes to specify a smooth path
It produces infinite acceleration at keyframe joints, causing jerky motion
It is computationally too expensive for real-time applications
It cannot interpolate rotations, only positions
questions.intuition: Velocity is the derivative of position. Piecewise linear means position has sharp corners at keyframes — the derivative (velocity) has discontinuous jumps there. A discontinuous velocity means infinite acceleration at that instant. Physically and visually, this is a sudden jerk — not smooth motion.
questions.explanation: At [22:10], from the slide: "Piecewise linear interpolation: simple, but yields rather rough motion (infinite acceleration)." The slope (velocity) changes instantaneously at each keyframe knot, which means infinite acceleration at those points. This motivates using smooth polynomial splines instead.

questions.question: What is a spline, and what is its historical origin?
options: A mathematical function defined by Fourier series; originated in signal processing
A parametric curve defined by control points; originated from Bézier's work at Renault
A recursive subdivision curve; originated from de Casteljau's algorithm at Citroën
Any piecewise polynomial function; originated from thin flexible strips of wood/metal used by draftsmen
questions.explanation: At [20:57], the lecturer states: "Mathematical theory of interpolation arose from study of thin strips of wood or metal ('splines') under various forces." A spline is any piecewise polynomial function. The physical spline — a flexible strip bent by ducks (weights) placed along a drawing board — naturally produces the minimum-curvature curve that passes through the specified points.

questions.question: What does it mean for a spline to "interpolate" data?
options: Tangents only, not positions
Approximates data, no exact fit
Passes through all knot points
Weighted average blending
questions.explanation: From slide 34: "Interpolates just means that the function exactly passes through those values." This is the key distinction: interpolation (exact pass-through) vs. approximation (close but not exact, as in B-splines). Keyframe animation typically needs interpolation — the character must be in the exact specified pose at the specified time.

questions.question: Why are cubic polynomials (degree 3) the most common choice for splines?
options: Minimizes bending energy norm
Lowest degree matching pos/deriv
Only polynomials with C2 continuity
Highest degree GPU-evaluable
questions.intuition: A physical spline (flexible wood strip) takes the shape that minimizes elastic bending energy — which mathematically is the integral of (curvature)² ≈ integral of (second derivative)². The exact solution under small-displacement assumptions is a piecewise cubic. Nature chose cubics to minimize bending; we choose them for the same reason.
questions.explanation: From slide 35: "Piecewise cubics give the exact solution to the elastic spline problem under assumption of small displacements. More precisely: among all curves interpolating a set of data points, cubics minimize the norm of the second derivative." They also have 4 DOFs — exactly enough to match position and derivative at both endpoints of each segment.

questions.question: What is the Runge phenomenon?
options: B-spline non-interpolation artifact
Overshoot from high tangents
Floating-point cancellation error
Runge oscillation in high-degree
questions.explanation: At [27:52], the lecturer warns: "It's really tempting to use a higher-degree polynomial for higher continuity, but this can lead to oscillation — ultimately a worse approximation." Slide 36 illustrates this: a high-degree polynomial fitted to uniformly spaced points oscillates wildly near the edges. This is why piecewise low-degree (cubic) splines are preferred over one high-degree polynomial.

questions.question: How many degrees of freedom does a cubic polynomial have, and what does that mean for fitting?
options: 6 DOFs — fully determined by position/derivative matches
4 DOFs — four coefficients; two used for endpoints, two free
3 DOFs — position + derivative at one end, position at other
2 DOFs — only one position and one derivative
questions.explanation: From slide 38: "Cubic polynomial has four degrees of freedom (DOFs), namely four coefficients (a,b,c,d). Only need two degrees of freedom to specify endpoints. Overall, four unknowns but only two equations — hence many solutions." The two remaining DOFs can be pinned by also specifying derivatives at the endpoints (Hermite) or by additional smoothness conditions (natural spline).

questions.question: What is a natural spline and how does it fix the remaining degrees of freedom?
options: First/last segments linear
Catenary hanging-chain model
Tangents point to neighbors
Zero curvature at both ends
questions.explanation: At [40:19], the lecturer explains: "One thing I could do is pin down the remaining degrees of freedom by setting the curvature to zero at the endpoints — just saying when I enter or exit the curve I'm going straight. Curvature here really means the second derivative, and that's why we call this a natural spline." Setting d²p/dt² = 0 at both ends adds 2 equations to close the system.

questions.question: What are the three desirable properties of a spline, and how does the natural spline perform?
options: Speed, accuracy, simplicity
Interp, continuity, locality — no interp
Interp, diff, efficiency — no eff
Interp, continuity, locality — no local
questions.intuition: "Locality" means moving one keyframe only affects the nearby curve. Natural splines solve one global linear system for all segments simultaneously — so moving one keyframe reshapes the entire curve. That's nonlocal. This matters in animation: if you adjust a pose at frame 100, you don't want poses at frames 1-99 to change.
questions.explanation: From slide 42: "INTERPOLATION: spline passes exactly through data points ✓. CONTINUITY: at least twice differentiable everywhere ✓. LOCALITY: moving one control point doesn't affect whole curve ✗." Natural splines solve a global system, so every segment is coupled — non-local behavior.

questions.question: What is a Hermite spline and how is it specified?
options: Defined by curvature at endpoints; tangents via integration
Defined by knot positions; tangents auto-computed from neighbors
Defined by four control points; passes through first/last only
Defined by endpoint positions AND tangents
questions.explanation: From slide 43: "Each cubic 'piece' specified by endpoints and tangents (Hermite form). Equivalently: by four points (Bézier form) — just take the difference!" The artist explicitly controls tangent directions at each keyframe, giving precise control over how the curve enters and exits each pose. 4 values (p0, p1, v0, v1) exactly determine the 4 cubic coefficients.

questions.question: How does the Hermite spline differ from the natural spline at joints between segments?
options: Hermite enforces C2; natural C1
Both enforce exactly C1 only
Natural enforces C2; Hermite C1
Hermite C0; natural C2
questions.explanation: From slide 44: "How is this different from our natural spline's tangent condition? There, tangents didn't have to match any prescribed value — they merely had to be the same on both sides (C1). Here, tangents must match given data." Natural splines additionally enforce C2 (curvature continuity) across joints; Hermite splines enforce only C1 (tangent continuity) since the user specifies potentially inconsistent tangents.

questions.question: What is a Catmull-Rom spline and what problem does it solve?
options: De Casteljau-defined recursive spline
B-spline variant with C2 continuity and local control
Interpolating B-spline passing through all control points
Hermite spline with tangents as neighbor differences
questions.intuition: Hermite splines require the animator to specify both positions AND tangent directions at every keyframe — that's twice the work. Catmull-Rom removes that burden: it computes the tangent at each keyframe automatically as (next_value - prev_value)/2. The artist only specifies where to be; the algorithm figures out how fast to get there.
questions.explanation: At [52:46], the lecturer explains: "Sometimes specifying tangents is annoying. Catmull-Rom: specialization of Hermite spline, determined by values alone. Basic idea: use difference of neighbors to define tangent." The tangent at point p_i is set to (p_{i+1} - p_{i-1})/2. This gives interpolation and C1 continuity with no extra input from the artist.

questions.question: What property does a B-spline sacrifice compared to natural and Hermite splines, and what does it gain?
options: Sacrifices continuity; gains exact interpolation through control points
Sacrifices computational efficiency; gains C3 continuity at all joints
Sacrifices exact interpolation (curve passes near but not through control points); gains better continuity and local control
Sacrifices locality; gains exact interpolation and C2 continuity
questions.explanation: From slide 47: "Get better continuity and local control by sacrificing interpolation." B-splines don't pass through their control points — the curve is merely attracted to them. In exchange, they provide local control (moving one control point only affects nearby segments) and higher continuity. The tradeoff table on slide 48 shows: natural (interp ✓, continuity ✓, local ✗), Hermite (interp ✓, continuity ✗, local ✓), B-splines (interp ✗, continuity ✓, local ✓).

questions.question: What does the "no free lunch" principle mean for splines?
options: Higher-degree splines are never worth using because of the Runge phenomenon
Every spline type requires the same computational cost regardless of its properties
Adding more control points always increases the computational cost superlinearly
No single spline type achieves all three desiderata simultaneously
questions.explanation: From slide 46/48, the comparison table shows: natural splines (interp ✓, continuity ✓, local ✗), Hermite (interp ✓, continuity ✓ only if tangents match, local ✓), B-splines (interp ✗, continuity ✓, local ✓). No row has all three checkmarks. The right choice depends on the application — illustration vs. animation vs. real-time rendering.

questions.question: What is being interpolated in a simple camera animation?
options: Projection matrix as 4×4 spline
Pos, view, up — each as spline
Focal length only; fixed pos
Position only; fixed look target
questions.explanation: From slide 50: "Animate position, direction, 'up' direction of camera — each path is a function f(t) = (x(t), y(t), z(t)) — each component (x,y,z) is a spline." Each scalar component is independently spline-interpolated. This is the most direct application of keyframing: the animator sets camera pose at key moments, splines fill in the continuous path.

questions.question: What is a kinematic chain (scene graph) and how is it used in character animation?
options: A chain of physics constraints linking rigid bodies; used for ragdoll simulation
A tree of transformations where child transformations are defined relative to parents; animated by interpolating each joint's rotation
A linked list of bones where each bone's position is independent of its neighbors
A sequence of keyframes linked by splines; the "chain" refers to temporal ordering
questions.intuition: Think of your arm: your forearm rotation is defined relative to your upper arm, which is relative to your shoulder, which is relative to your torso. The scene graph encodes exactly this hierarchy. To animate a waving hand, you only need to specify shoulder and elbow rotations — the hand position is automatically computed by chaining those transforms.
questions.explanation: From slide 51: "Scene graph/kinematic chain: scene as tree of transformations. E.g., in 'cube man,' configuration of a leg might be expressed as rotation relative to body. Animate by interpolating transformations." The animator keyframes joint rotations; the character's full pose is then computed by traversing the transformation tree.

questions.question: What is inverse kinematics (IK) and how does it differ from forward kinematics?
options: Forward kinematics: used for rigid bodies. IK: used only for deformable bodies
FK: joint angles → end-effector position. IK: end-effector goal → joint angles
Forward kinematics: physics drives joint motion. IK: artist specifies joint angles directly
Forward kinematics: works in 2D. IK: extends kinematics to 3D
questions.explanation: From slide 52: "Rather than adjust individual transformations, set 'goal' and use algorithm to come up with plausible motion. Many algorithms — basic idea: numerical optimization/descent." IK solves the inverse problem: given where you want the hand to be, find the shoulder/elbow/wrist angles that put it there. This is a numerical optimization problem (often nonlinear, with multiple solutions).

questions.question: What is skeletal animation and what problem does it solve?
options: Animating rigid skeleton pieces directly without any surface mesh
Procedurally generating skeleton structures from muscle simulation
Using a skeleton of bones to drive the deformation of a continuous surface mesh, with each vertex weighted by nearby bone influences
Capturing motion from a real actor's skeleton using reflective markers
questions.explanation: From slide 53: "Often use 'skeleton' to drive deformation of continuous surface mesh. Influence of each bone determined by, e.g., weighting function." Instead of animating every vertex of a mesh directly, the artist animates a sparse skeleton of bones. Each skin vertex moves as a weighted blend of its nearby bones' transformations — giving smooth, realistic deformation with far fewer controls.

questions.question: What are blend shapes and when are they used instead of skeletal animation?
options: Procedural noise functions blended together to create organic surface textures
Blending motion capture data from multiple actors to create new animations
Interpolating between pre-modeled shapes using spline-controlled blend weights
Physics-based blending of rigid body and soft body simulations
questions.explanation: From slide 54: "Instead of skeleton, interpolate directly between surfaces. E.g., model a collection of facial expressions. Simplest scheme: take linear combination of vertex positions. Spline used to control choice of blending weights." Blend shapes are commonly used for facial animation where the deformations are too complex for a skeletal rig — an artist models "happy," "sad," "surprised," etc., and the animator mixes between them.

questions.question: In a spline system, how does each constraint (e.g., matching a keyframe value) translate into a solvable system?
options: Constraints as penalty terms
Each constraint adds linear equality
Each constraint lowers degree by one
Each constraint adds nonlinear equation
questions.explanation: From slide 40: "Each condition on the spline leads to a linear equality. If we have m degrees of freedom, we need m (linearly independent) conditions. We can express this as a matrix equation Ax = b." This is the key insight: spline fitting is just linear algebra. Each keyframe position, tangent match, or curvature condition is one row in a linear system.

questions.question: Why is piecewise polynomial interpolation preferred over using one single high-degree polynomial?
options: High-degree polynomials cannot satisfy C2 continuity conditions
The rendering pipeline only supports polynomials up to degree 3
A single high-degree polynomial risks the Runge phenomenon
High-degree polynomials can only be evaluated at integer time steps
questions.explanation: From slides 33 and 36: "Common interpolant: piecewise polynomial 'spline' — basic motivation: get better continuity than piecewise linear." And on Runge: "Tempting to use higher-degree polynomials for higher continuity, but can lead to oscillation — ultimately worse approximation." Piecewise cubics achieve C2 continuity with local, stable behavior.

questions.question: What is a zoetrope and what principle does it demonstrate?
options: A 3D printer that creates solid objects by layering cross-sections
A spinning cylinder with sequential images viewed through slits
A hand-cranked camera that captures motion at 24 frames per second
An early computer monitor that displayed animation by scanning electron beams
questions.explanation: At [11:04], the lecturer describes: "Here we have a solid object with pieces arranged on a spinning plate. A strobe light flashes, and you see the different stages of motion frozen in time, creating an animation." The zoetrope exploits the beta phenomenon — successive static images, presented quickly enough, are perceived as continuous motion by the brain.

questions.question: What pattern appears repeatedly in the history of both film and computer animation?
options: Animation technologies always emerge first in scientific research before entertainment adoption
Each new animation technology first emerged as a scientific tool, then was adopted for entertainment
Historically, every major animation technique was invented by university researchers and only later licensed to Hollywood studios
The timeline of animation tech development shows consistent precedence of academic labs over industry R&D departments
questions.explanation: From slides 9 and 14: Film — "Originally used as scientific tool rather than for entertainment. Critical technology that accelerated development of animation." Computer animation — "New technology, also developed as a scientific tool. Again turbo-charged the development of animation." Muybridge was settling a scientific bet; Sutherland was studying human-computer interaction; both tools became the foundation of modern animation.

questions.question: What distinguishes a Bézier spline from a Hermite spline, mathematically?
options: Bézier enforces C2 continuity; Hermite enforces only C0 continuity
Bézier uses trigonometric basis functions; Hermite uses polynomial basis functions
Bézier interpolates all four control points; Hermite interpolates only the endpoints
Bézier specifies the curve by four control points (two endpoints + two "pull" points); Hermite specifies by endpoints and explicit tangent vectors — they encode the same information differently
questions.explanation: From slide 43: "Each cubic piece specified by endpoints and tangents (Hermite). Equivalently: by four points (Bézier form) — just take the difference!" The Bézier "handle" control points encode the tangent direction and magnitude. Hermite tangent vector = 3 × (Bézier control point − endpoint). They're the same mathematical object, just written in different bases.

questions.question: Why are Catmull-Rom splines particularly useful for animation compared to Hermite splines?
options: They compute tangents automatically from keyframe differences
They are the only splines that can handle non-uniform time spacing between keyframes
They always produce C2-continuous curves, unlike Hermite splines which only guarantee C1
They use fewer control points per segment, making them faster to evaluate
questions.explanation: From slide 45: "Sometimes makes sense to specify tangents (e.g., illustration). Often more convenient to just specify values. Catmull-Rom: specialization of Hermite spline, determined by values alone. Basic idea: use difference of neighbors to define tangent." For character animation, Catmull-Rom means the animator just places poses at keyframes — no need to manually tune tangent handles.

questions.question: In character animation, why is interpolating joint rotations preferred over interpolating joint positions directly?
options: Only rotations need keyframing — positions are implicit
Interpolating positions causes the Runge phenomenon; rotations are immune to this
Rotations are always easier to interpolate than positions
Positions can only be interpolated linearly; rotations support spline interpolation
questions.explanation: From slide 51: "Configuration of a leg might be expressed as rotation relative to body. Animate by interpolating transformations." In a kinematic chain, the world-space position of every joint is determined by the chain of parent rotations from the root. So to animate the whole character, you only need to keyframe rotations — positions follow automatically from the hierarchy.

questions.question: What was the Phenakistoscope and why was it significant?
options: A spinning disc with sequential images viewed through slits
An early projector that displayed animation on a wall for an audience
A zoetrope variant that used mirrors instead of slits to view the animation
The first motion picture camera, which recorded images at 12 frames per second
questions.explanation: At [02:53], the lecturer describes: "One of the first technological developments pushing toward animation was the Phenakistoscope — you have a sequence of images on a spinning disc, played back by spinning and watching through a small slit." It exploits the beta phenomenon to create perceived motion. Along with the zoetrope, it established the core principle of all film and animation: rapid sequential static images create perceived motion.

questions.question: What does the B-spline basis being "defined recursively" mean in practice?
options: Each B-spline basis function is a linear blend of two lower-degree basis functions
B-spline evaluation requires a recursive tree traversal with exponential time complexity
B-splines are defined by subdividing control polygons recursively, like Catmull-Clark surfaces
B-splines are computed by recursive neural networks that learn the optimal shape from data
questions.intuition: The recursion is: a degree-0 B-spline is just a box function (1 inside an interval, 0 outside). A degree-1 B-spline blends two adjacent box functions linearly — giving a tent function. A degree-2 blends two tent functions — giving a smoother bump. Each degree-up smooths the previous. This is why higher-degree B-splines are smoother: each recursion level adds one more convolution with a box, which smooths.
questions.explanation: From slide 47: "B-spline basis defined recursively: linear interpolation [between shifted lower-degree bases]. B-spline itself is then a linear combination of these bases." The recursive definition ensures each basis function has compact support (affects only a local range of the parameter), which is what gives B-splines their locality property.
